mainTopic: Vows between courtyard partners, rented-out property, 'your house' versus 'this house', and whether the חכמים argue when partners forbade each other
overview: This amud finishes the משנה about partners in a shared courtyard (חצר) when a נדר forbids benefit between them. Neither partner may set up a mill or an oven, or raise chickens, there. When only one partner is forbidden, or when an outsider is forbidden from one partner, the תנא קמא says he may not enter. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב allows him to enter, because he can say he is walking in a part that does not belong to the one he is forbidden from. The משנה also says the court forces the one who vowed to sell his share. Next comes a rented-out bathhouse or olive press: using it is forbidden only if the owner still keeps a hold in it. Then the משנה teaches that a vow against 'your house' ends when the owner dies or sells it, while a vow against 'this house' stays in force. The גמרא asks whether the courtyard argument also applies when the partners forbade each other. It shows that the משנה speaks about a partner who banned himself (נדור), so the משנה does not settle that question. Finally, רבה begins to report a teaching from זעירי, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Both partners may not set up a mill, an oven, or chickens
steps.stepSummary: Two partners are each forbidden by a נדר from benefiting from the other. Neither one may set up a mill or an oven, or raise chickens, in their shared courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: And both of them are forbidden to set up a mill or an oven, or to raise chickens, in the shared courtyard.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes its first case: two partners who are both forbidden from benefiting from each other. It names uses of the courtyard that neither of them may make.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Walking in the courtyard was already discussed and disputed. Here the משנה lists heavier, ongoing uses: a mill, an oven, or chickens. Neither partner may make these uses in the shared space.

phrases.english: And both of them are forbidden
phrases.notes: This means the two partners who share the courtyard, when each is forbidden by a נדר from benefiting from the other.

phrases.english: to set up a mill and an oven
and to raise chickens.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה about two partners who are forbidden from benefiting from each other.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Neither partner may set up a mill or an oven, or raise chickens, in the shared courtyard.

steps.title: Only one partner is forbidden: he may not enter
steps.stepSummary: Now the vow goes only one way: one partner is forbidden from benefiting from the other. The תנא קמא rules that he may not enter the courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one of the partners was forbidden by a vow from benefiting from the other, he may not enter the courtyard.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה starts a new case. Only one partner is forbidden from benefiting from the other, and the first opinion says he may not even walk into the courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each partner owns a share of the whole courtyard. So when the forbidden partner walks anywhere in it, he is also using the other partner's share, and that counts as forbidden benefit.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone forbidden by a vow from getting benefit
A courtyard shared by the homes around it

phrases.english: If one of them was
forbidden by a vow from benefiting from his fellow,
he may not enter the courtyard.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיָה אֶחָד מֵהֶם מוּדָּר הֲנָאָה מֵחֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from a vow that goes both ways to a vow that goes only one way.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The partner who is forbidden may not enter the shared courtyard.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב: he enters only his own part
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב disagrees. The forbidden partner may enter, because he can say he is walking only in his own share.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says: he can say to his partner, 'I am entering into my own part, and I am not entering into yours.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב argues with the opinion before him and allows the forbidden partner to enter the courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He sees the courtyard differently. The forbidden partner can treat the space he walks in as his own share, so he is not using his partner's property at all.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says,
he can say to him:
Into my own part I am entering,
and I am not entering into yours.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר, יָכוֹל הוּא לוֹמַר לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an opinion that disagrees with step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The forbidden partner may enter, because he says he is using only his own share.

steps.title: The court forces the one who vowed to sell his share
steps.stepSummary: The court pushes the partner who made the vow to sell his share of the courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the court forces the one who made the vow to sell his share.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a practical fix for this partnership: the court makes the one who vowed sell his share.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two partners cannot easily share a courtyard when a vow stands between them. So the court makes the partner who made the vow sell his share, and the problem is gone.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who made the vow

steps.confusionAlert: Be careful: the משנה says the court forces הנודר, the one who made the vow. He is the forbidden partner himself. The גמרא in Step 12 uses this word to show he banned himself, so he caused his own problem.

phrases.english: And they force the one who made the vow
to sell his share.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכוֹפִין אֶת הַנּוֹדֵר לִמְכּוֹר אֶת חֶלְקוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a practical step that applies to the case of one partner forbidden from the other.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The one who made the vow is forced to sell his share of the courtyard.

steps.title: An outsider forbidden from one partner may not enter
steps.stepSummary: An outsider from the marketplace is forbidden by a vow from benefiting from one of the partners. The תנא קמא says he may not enter their courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone from the marketplace is forbidden by a vow from benefiting from one of the partners, he may not enter the courtyard.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings a third case. Now the forbidden person is a stranger, and the first opinion again forbids him to enter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The courtyard belongs partly to the partner he is forbidden from. So walking anywhere in it means using some of that partner's property.

keyTerms.meaning: From the marketplace: an outsider who is not one of the partners

phrases.english: If one from the marketplace was
forbidden by a vow from benefit from one of them,
he may not enter the courtyard.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיָה אֶחָד מִן הַשּׁוּק מוּדָּר בְּאֶחָד מֵהֶם הֲנָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves the same question over to an outsider instead of a partner.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The outsider may not enter the shared courtyard.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב: he enters only the other partner's part
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב allows the outsider to enter. He can say he is walking in the other partner's share.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says: he can say to him, 'I am entering into your fellow's part, and I am not entering into yours.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב uses the same reasoning as before and allows the outsider to enter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the partner said 'I walk in my own part.' Here the outsider says 'I walk in the other partner's part.' Either way, he is not using the property of the person he is forbidden from.
steps.whatToRemember: In each courtyard case, the תנא קמא forbids entering. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב allows it, because the person can say he is walking in a part that does not belong to the one he is forbidden from.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says,
he can say to him:
Into your fellow's part I am entering,
phrases.notes: Your fellow means the other partner, the one he is allowed to benefit from.

phrases.english: and I am not entering into yours.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר, יָכוֹל לוֹמַר לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with step 5, using the same reasoning as step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The outsider may enter, because he says he is using only the other partner's share.

steps.title: A rented-out bathhouse or olive press
steps.stepSummary: Someone is forbidden from benefiting from a person who owns a bathhouse or olive press that is rented out in the city. Using it is forbidden only if the owner still keeps a hold in it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone is forbidden by a vow from benefiting from another person, and that person has a bathhouse or an olive press rented out in the city: if he still has a hold in them, it is forbidden. If he has no hold in them, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה starts a new case about property that the owner has rented out to someone else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the property is rented out, the question is whether the owner still has a real stake in it. If he keeps some hold, using the place still benefits him, so it is forbidden. If he has no hold, the place really belongs to the renter for now, so it is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: A hold: the owner still keeps some stake in the property

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a clear test. Property the owner has fully rented out is no longer treated as his for the vow; it still counts as his only if he keeps a real hold in it.

phrases.english: One forbidden by a vow from benefiting from his fellow
and he has a bathhouse and an olive press
phrases.notes: 'He' is the friend, the owner the other person isn't allowed to benefit from.

phrases.english: rented out in the city,

phrases.aramaic: אִם יֵשׁ לוֹ בָּהֶן תְּפִיסַת יָד — אָסוּר,
phrases.english: if he has a hold in them, it is forbidden,

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לוֹ בָּהֶן תְּפִיסַת יָד — מוּתָּר.
phrases.english: if he has no hold in them, it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַמּוּדָּר הֲנָאָה מֵחֲבֵירוֹ וְיֵשׁ לוֹ מֶרְחָץ וּבֵית הַבַּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about rented-out property instead of a shared courtyard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Using the place is forbidden if the owner keeps a hold in it, and permitted if he does not.

steps.title: Vowing off 'your house' versus 'this house'
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a vow against 'your house' or 'your field' ends when the owner dies or sells. A vow against 'this house' or 'this field' stays in force even after that.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says to his friend, 'Entering your house is קונם for me' or 'Buying your field is קונם for me', and the friend dies or sells it to someone else, it becomes permitted. If he said 'Entering this house is קונם' or 'Buying this field is קונם', it stays forbidden even if the owner dies or sells it.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a new rule. It depends on whether the vow was tied to the person ('your house') or to the object itself ('this house').
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Your house' links the ban to the friend's ownership, so once he no longer owns it, the vow has nothing to hold on to. 'This house' links the ban to the building itself, so a change of owner does not matter.

keyTerms.meaning: A vow word that makes something forbidden like a קרבן
This house (tied to the object itself)
He sold it to someone else

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a basic idea in vows: the exact words decide what the vow is attached to, the person or the object.

phrases.english: One who says to his friend:
"Entering your house is קונם for me,
or buying your field",
if he died or sold it to another, it is permitted.
phrases.notes: 'He' here is the owner of the house or field, not the one who made the vow.

phrases.english: "Entering this house is קונם for me,"
or "buying this field",
if he died or sold it to another, it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ קֻוֽנָּם לְבֵיתְךָ שֶׁאֲנִי נִכְנָס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case in the משנה, after the bathhouse and olive press rule in Step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Your house' or 'your field' becomes permitted after the owner dies or sells. 'This house' or 'this field' stays forbidden.

steps.title: Do the חכמים disagree even when the partners forbade each other?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the courtyard argument applies only when each partner vowed on himself, or also when each one forbade the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: they argue when the partners vowed on themselves. What if each partner forbade the other? Do we say they argue only when each vowed on himself, but when they forbade each other the חכמים agree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, because the partners are like people who were forced? Or perhaps the חכמים argue even when they forbade each other?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the courtyard argument between the partners in the משנה (see Steps 2–3). It asks whether that argument covers a case where the ban came from the other partner and not from oneself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If you vowed on yourself, you caused your own problem, so the חכמים can be strict. If someone else put the ban on you, you are an אנוס, meaning it is not your fault. Maybe then the חכמים would accept רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's lenient approach.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised for them
People who are forced, not at fault

steps.confusionAlert: נדר means 'I banned myself.' הדיר means 'I banned someone else.' The whole question depends on this difference.

phrases.english: GEMARA: A question was raised before them:
They disagree where the partners vowed,
but if they forbade one another, what is the law?
Do we say: it is only where they vowed that they disagree,
but where they forbade one another

phrases.aramaic: מוֹדוּ לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן לְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב
phrases.english: the Rabbis agree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב
because they are like people who were forced?
Or perhaps:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ בְּהִדִּירוּ זֶה אֶת זֶה פְּלִיגִי רַבָּנַן?
phrases.english: even where they forbade one another, the Rabbis disagree?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ בְּנָדְרוּ פְּלִיגִי הִדִּירוּ זֶה אֶת זֶה מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the house and field case to the courtyard argument earlier in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the argument between the חכמים and רבי אליעזר בן יעקב also apply when the ban came from the other partner?

steps.title: Proof from the word 'מודר' in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a proof from the משנה's wording 'מודר', which sounds like someone else forbade him, and still the חכמים are strict.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'If one of them was forbidden by a vow from benefiting from his friend', and the חכמים disagree!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question from the משנה's own words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'מודר' suggests the partner was banned by the other's vow. Even so, the חכמים forbid him to enter. That would mean they argue even when he is an אנוס.

keyTerms.meaning: Forbidden from benefit, banned by someone else's vow

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If one of them was
forbidden by a vow from benefiting from his friend,
phrases.notes: This quotes the courtyard case of the משנה from Step 2.

phrases.english: and the Rabbis disagree!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע הָיָה אֶחָד מֵהֶן מוּדָּר הֲנָאָה מֵחֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question of Step 9.
steps.raayaObject: The חכמים argue even when the partner was forbidden by the other.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's word 'מודר' in the courtyard case.

steps.title: Read the משנה as 'נדור': he vowed on himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes off the proof by reading the משנה as 'נדור', meaning the partner banned himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Teach it as: 'he vowed not to benefit from his friend.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from Step 10 by changing how the משנה is read.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read as 'נדור', the משנה speaks only about a partner who banned himself. So it tells us nothing about a partner banned by someone else, and the question of Step 9 stays open.

phrases.english: Teach: he vowed not to benefit from his friend.
phrases.notes: The גמרא wants us to read the משנה as 'נדור' instead of 'מודר', so he's the one who banned himself.

steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Removes the proof without answering the question of Step 9.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof depended on reading 'מודר'. The משנה can be read as 'נדור'.

steps.title: Support for 'נדור': the court forces the vower to sell
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports reading 'נדור'. The משנה says the court forces the vower to sell his share, and that only makes sense if he caused his own problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too it makes sense, because the end of the משנה teaches: 'The court forces the one who vowed to sell his share.' If you say he vowed on himself, that explains why we force him. But if you say the other one forbade him, why force him? He is not at fault!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the reading from Step 11 using the rule from Step 4.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Forcing a sale is fair only for someone who brought the problem on himself. A person banned by another is an אנוס and would not be pushed to sell. So the משנה must be speaking about one who vowed on himself.

keyTerms.meaning: The end part of the משנה
He is completely forced, not at fault

steps.whatToRemember: The courtyard משנה speaks about a partner who banned himself (נדור). So the question of whether the חכמים would agree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב when he was banned by another (הדירו) is not answered by it.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule of forcing a sale shows that the משנה blames the vower. That limits the חכמים' strict view to someone who caused his own problem.

phrases.english: So too it is reasonable,
since the end of the משנה teaches:

phrases.aramaic: וְכוֹפִין אֶת הַנּוֹדֵר לִמְכּוֹר אֶת חֶלְקוֹ.
phrases.english: and the court forces the one who vowed to sell his share.
It works well if you say that he himself vowed,
that is why it teaches that the court forces him.
But if you say that the other forbade him by a vow,
why does the court force him?
He is forced and not at fault!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the reading given in Step 11.
steps.raayaObject: The courtyard משנה speaks about one who vowed on himself (נדור).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The end of the משנה: the court forces the vower to sell his share.

steps.title: רבה introduces a teaching from זעירי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new statement: רבה passes along something he learned from זעירי. The content of the teaching follows right after.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move by introducing a new teaching that רבה heard from זעירי. The actual ruling comes in the next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof-and-rejection cycle about 'נדור' and 'מודר' is now finished, and the גמרא turns to a fresh teaching about the courtyard case in the משנה. The double 'אמר' tells us there is a chain: זעירי taught it, and רבה reports it. On its own this line gives no ruling. It only tells us whose words are coming.

keyTerms.meaning: 'So-and-so said that so-and-so said.' This is a chain of reporting: the second name is the original source

steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for a ruling in this line. It only introduces the speaker. The teaching itself starts in the next line.

phrases.english: Rabba said that Ze'eiri said:

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: Setup line for the next מימרא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof cycle in steps 9-12 ends, this line opens a new teaching about the courtyard case in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This line only introduces a teaching of זעירי, reported by רבה, which comes in the next line.
